passage_text: Researchers at the University of Westfield conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled study to examine the impact of caffeine consumption on reaction time across different age groups. A total of 300 participants were recruited and divided into three age categories: 18‑30 (Young), 31‑50 (Middle), and 51‑70 (Elderly). Each participant completed a standardized computerized reaction time test after ingesting either a placebo or a 200‑mg caffeine dose, to which they were randomly assigned. The mean reaction times (in milliseconds) and standard deviations were recorded, along with the sample size for each group. The study aimed to determine whether caffeine’s stimulatory effects on cognitive processing vary with age, potentially informing guidelines for safe caffeine intake in older adults. The data presented in Table 1 below summarize the key findings of the reaction time measurements for the placebo and caffeine conditions across the three age groups.
stem: Which of the following best describes the pattern of caffeine’s effect on reaction time across the age groups?

options.A: Caffeine improves reaction time equally in all age groups.
options.B: Caffeine improves reaction time most in the Young group and by a smaller, similar amount in the Middle and Elderly groups.
options.C: Caffeine improves reaction time only in the Elderly group.
options.D: Caffeine has no effect on reaction time in any age group.

explanation: Reaction times fall in all groups; the improvement is greatest in the Young group (30 ms) and smaller and equal in the Middle and Elderly groups (20 ms each).
trap: Seeing that caffeine lowered reaction time in every age group and assuming the benefit was the same size, without computing the 30, 20 and 20 ms differences.

stem: Which experimental design would best isolate caffeine’s effect on reaction time while controlling for individual variability?

options.A: A between-subjects design where each participant receives either placebo or caffeine.
options.B: A within-subjects crossover design where each participant receives both placebo and caffeine on separate days.
options.C: A longitudinal cohort study following participants over 5 years.
options.D: A case‑control study comparing caffeine users to non‑users.

explanation: A within‑subject crossover design controls for inter‑individual differences by having each participant serve as their own control, reducing variability and increasing statistical power.
trap: Choosing the between-subjects design actually used in the study, which leaves person-to-person differences in baseline speed in the error term.

stem: Calculate the overall mean reduction in reaction time after caffeine ingestion across all age groups.
trap: Reporting the Young group's 30 ms reduction alone, or rounding the average up to 25 ms, instead of computing (30 + 20 + 20)/3 = 23.3 ms.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage or Table 1?

options.A: Mean reaction time was lower with caffeine than with placebo in every age group.
options.B: The sample sizes are equal across age groups.
options.D: The study used a double‑blind design.

explanation: Correct: D) The passage does not mention blinding of participants or investigators. Why the others are wrong: A) Caffeine means (290, 330, 360) are below placebo means (320, 350, 380) in all groups. B) Each group has n = 100. C) SDs are 15, 20 and 25 ms for Young, Middle and Elderly.
trap: Assuming a placebo-controlled study must also be double-blind.

stem: Which statement about the percent reduction in mean reaction time with caffeine is correct?

options.A: It was greater in the Young group (about 9.4%) than in the Elderly group (about 5.3%).
options.B: It was greater in the Elderly group than in the Young group.
options.C: It was greater in the Middle group than in the Young group.
options.D: It was the same in all three age groups.

explanation: Correct: A) Young: 30/320 = 9.4%; Middle: 20/350 = 5.7%; Elderly: 20/380 = 5.3%. Why the others are wrong: B) Elderly (5.3%) was smaller than Young (9.4%). C) Middle (5.7%) was smaller than Young (9.4%). D) The three percentages differ.
trap: Comparing absolute reductions of 20 ms in Middle and Elderly groups and concluding the percent reductions are the same.
